- If sentiment is positive (≥0.2) and forecast is rising steadily, reduce forecast slope to avoid over-optimism.  
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.0) and forecast is falling, increase forecast slope to avoid underreaction.  
- After a sharp price spike, model tends to overcorrect — reduce forecast slope for 3–5 days post-spike.  
- When true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive drops from peak), model often fails to adjust — apply downward bias correction.  
- If sentiment is neutral (0.0) and forecast is flat, check for horizon mismatch — true outcomes often show volatility; adjust for 1–2 day lag in model response.  
- In low-sentiment periods, model often underestimates downside risk — add 2–3% downward buffer to forecast if sentiment ≤0.0.  
- If model forecast is consistently above true outcome (e.g., >10% over 30d), reduce forecast by 5–10% for next horizon if sentiment is weak or neutral.  
- If sentiment history shows repeated 0.2 spikes followed by sharp drops, model tends to overpredict recovery — reduce forecast by 3–5% after 2 consecutive 0.2 sentiment days.
